transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I guess my wife is the main reason I'm here. I know she says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

Which, you know, direct communication is just so rare these days. I tell my undergraduate students that all the time—I'm a teaching assistant over at the university, mostly handling the freshman seminars right now. Trying to get 18-year-olds to actually engage in a discussion is like pulling teeth. Just last Tuesday, I stood at the front of the room for five whole minutes in complete silence, just waiting for someone, anyone, to answer a basic question about the printing press. You'd think they don't even do the assigned reading before they show up. The university changed the whole syllabus structure back in the fall to try and help with student retention, but honestly, it just means more grading for me. 

But anyway, I... what was I saying? Right, my wife. The messages. I just can't shake the feeling that they aren't an accident.
Have you ever been told by a doctor that you have any significant medical conditions, or have you recently started taking any new medications or substances?

No, I don't have any medical conditions. I haven't started taking anything new, either. No medications. Well, I mean, I drink a lot of coffee, if you count that as a substance. Honestly, probably too much lately because they finally fixed the espresso machine in the graduate lounge. 

It was broken for a solid three months, and we had to keep walking all the way over to the student union just to get a decent cup. If you want to see pure chaos, try navigating a campus coffee shop at 10 AM on a Thursday. It’s just a sea of laptops and 18-year-olds drinking these massive, sugary iced lattes. I really don't understand how they can consume that much sugar and still manage to fall asleep during my seminar. It honestly defies biology. The university's dining services contract is actually up for renewal next spring, and there's this whole massive debate going on about whether they're going to bring in a different vendor. I really hope they do, because the pastries they stock are always stale by Tuesday, and the prices are just extortionate for grad students. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, medical stuff. No, I'm completely healthy. No prescriptions or anything like that.
Do you ever hear sounds or voices that other people around you cannot hear?

No, I don't hear anything like that. No voices or strange sounds. Honestly, the only thing I hear that other people don't seem to notice is the hum of the fluorescent lights in the seminar rooms. It's this low, constant buzzing that drives me absolutely up the wall. I put in a maintenance request about it back in October, but you know how university facilities are. They came in, looked at the fixture for maybe thirty seconds, said it was "operating within normal parameters," and just left. 

Normal parameters, right. It's like the administration just doesn't care about the learning environment. They just spent three million dollars renovating the athletic center—brand new weight rooms, state-of-the-art turf on the practice field—but they can't be bothered to replace a buzzing lightbulb in a room where we're supposed to be discussing the Enlightenment. It's all about optics and donor money. I was talking to one of the older professors about it, Dr. Henderson, and he said it's been like this since the 90s. He actually remembers when they built that wing of the humanities building, and apparently, the contractor they used was... 

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling. You asked about voices, right? No, nothing like that. Just the lights.
Aside from your concerns about your wife's messages, have you ever felt that your thoughts were being controlled, broadcasted to others, or that you were losing your grip on reality in any other way?

No, no, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own. I definitely don't feel like anyone is controlling me or reading my mind. I mean, if people could read my mind, I think I'd be out of a job pretty quickly, given what I think about the administration half the time. 

Speaking of the administration, you wouldn't believe the email they sent out yesterday about the new parking regulations. It's like they actively want to make it impossible for graduate students to commute. They've raised the permit fees by twenty percent, and they've reallocated half the commuter lot to "visitor parking," which is just ridiculous because we hardly get any visitors on that side of campus anyway. It's just a cash grab, plain and simple. I was talking to Sarah, another TA in the history department, and she's thinking about organizing a petition. She actually organized one last year when they tried to cut our printing quota, and it worked, but parking is a whole different beast. The university makes so much money off those tickets. I got one last month when I was parked for literally three minutes while I ran into the library to drop off a book. Three minutes! The meter maid must have been hiding in the bushes. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my mind. Yeah, no, my thoughts are perfectly normal. I'm not losing my grip on reality or anything. Just dealing with my wife and... well, and the parking situation.

latest_inference.note: The patient exhibits a persistent, systematized delusional belief regarding his wife's messages (delusion of reference/infidelity) for over a year, while explicitly denying hallucinations, thought broadcasting, or other disorganized symptoms characteristic of F20.0 or F23. His speech, while tangential, does not show the profound formal thought disorder or functional decline required for schizophrenia.
